name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_SEQ_Q01 - Chronological stages in the life cycle of Plasmodium

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following stages of the life cycle of Plasmodium in the correct chronological sequence, starting from the entry of the parasite into the human body:

(i) Rupture of red blood cells releasing haemozoin and causing recurring fever
(ii) Bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito injecting sporozoites into human blood
(iii) Fertilisation and development in the mosquito's gut followed by migration of sporozoites to salivary glands
(iv) Asexual multiplication of the parasite within human liver cells
(v) Uptake of gametocytes by a female Anopheles mosquito during a blood meal

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plasmodium is a digenetic protozoan parasite that requires both a human host and a female Anopheles mosquito host to complete its life cycle.

Step 2: Chronological Reconstruction of Stages
1. Infection begins when an infected female Anopheles mosquito bites a human and injects sporozoites (the infectious form) into the bloodstream.
2. The sporozoites travel through blood to the liver and multiply asexually within the liver cells.
3. After bursting out of liver cells, the parasites attack red blood cells (RBCs), multiply asexually, and rupture the RBCs, releasing the toxic substance haemozoin that causes recurring chill and high fever; gametocytes also develop in RBCs.
4. When another female Anopheles mosquito bites the infected person, it takes up the gametocytes with its blood meal.
5. Inside the mosquito, fertilisation and further development occur in the gut, and mature sporozoites migrate to the salivary glands ready to infect a new human host.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence starts with mosquito bite injecting sporozoites, followed by multiplication in liver cells, rupture of RBCs releasing haemozoin, uptake of gametocytes by the mosquito, and finally fertilisation in the mosquito's gut with migration of sporozoites to salivary glands.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_SEQ_Q02 - Sequential events in HIV infection and AIDS progression

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events occurring during HIV infection and progression to AIDS in the correct chronological order:

(i) Incorporation of viral DNA into the host cell's DNA
(ii) Progressive decrease in the number of helper T-lymphocytes (\(\mathrm{T_H}\)), leading to opportunistic infections
(iii) Entry of HIV into macrophages and synthesis of viral DNA from viral RNA by reverse transcriptase
(iv) Production of progeny viruses that are released into the blood and attack other helper T-lymphocytes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
HIV is an enveloped retrovirus with an RNA genome that replicates inside host immune cells (macrophages and helper T-lymphocytes) via a DNA intermediate.

Step 2: Chronological Reconstruction of Events
1. After entering the human body, HIV enters macrophages where its RNA genome replicates to form viral DNA using the enzyme reverse transcriptase.
2. This newly formed viral DNA incorporates into the host cell's DNA and directs the infected cell to produce virus particles (making macrophages an HIV factory).
3. Simultaneously, HIV enters helper T-lymphocytes (\(\mathrm{T_H}\)), replicates, and releases progeny viruses into the blood, which then attack other helper T-lymphocytes.
4. Repetition of this cycle causes a progressive decline in helper T-lymphocytes, rendering the patient immuno-deficient and vulnerable to opportunistic infections by Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi, and Toxoplasma.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence proceeds from viral entry into macrophages and reverse transcription of viral RNA to viral DNA, to incorporation of viral DNA into the host genome, to release of progeny viruses attacking helper T-lymphocytes, and finally to progressive depletion of helper T-lymphocytes causing opportunistic infections.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_HUMANHEALTHANDDISEASE_SEQ_Q03 - Sequence of immune events in vaccination and memory

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps involved in active immunisation (vaccination) and subsequent protection against a pathogen in the correct logical sequence:

(i) Rapid recognition of the pathogen by memory B and T-cells during a subsequent exposure
(ii) Introduction of antigenic proteins or inactivated/weakened pathogen into the body
(iii) Low-intensity primary immune response and generation of memory B and T-cells
(iv) Highly intensified secondary (anamnestic) response with massive antibody production overwhelming the invaders

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The principle of vaccination and immunisation is based on the 'memory' property of the acquired immune system, mediated by B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes.

Step 2: Chronological Reconstruction of Steps
1. During vaccination, a preparation of antigenic proteins of a pathogen or inactivated/weakened pathogen (vaccine) is introduced into the body.
2. This first encounter elicits a low-intensity primary immune response that produces antibodies against the antigens and generates memory B and T-cells.
3. On a subsequent actual exposure to the same pathogen, the memory B and T-cells recognise the pathogen quickly.
4. This rapid recognition triggers a highly intensified secondary (anamnestic) response, overwhelming the invaders with a massive production of antibodies.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct logical sequence moves from vaccine introduction, to primary immune response and generation of memory B and T-cells, to rapid recognition upon subsequent exposure, and finally to the highly intensified secondary response with massive antibody production.
